editions.resume: The first transatlantic race shattered preconceived notions. Thirty-eight competitors set sail, barely a quarter of them on racing boats. Olivier de Kersauson, Philippe Poupon, Florence Arthaud, and Bruno Peyron were among the entrants. Manureva went silent, and navigator Alain Colas disappeared at sea. Olympus Photo, Mike Birch's small yellow trimaran, finished 98 seconds ahead of Michel Malinovsky's Kriter V after 23 days of racing.
editions.description: In response to the size restrictions imposed on boats following the 1976 Transatlantic Race, Parisian advertising executive Michel Etevenon officially presented the Route du Rhum course in May 1978. This was the first French solo transatlantic race, starting from Saint-Malo and finishing in Pointe-à-Pitre. The race was open to both monohulls and multihulls and had no size limit for the vessels. A total of 38 sailors, both professional and amateur, registered for this inaugural edition. Among them were big names in offshore racing and promising young talents: Mike Birch, Alain Colas, Florence Arthaud, Michel Malinovsky, Olivier de Kersauson, Philippe Poupon, Marc Pajot, Bruno Peyron, and others. The renowned Éric Tabarly was notably absent that year, having failed to secure the necessary funding in time. On November 5, 1978, the day of the grand departure arrived, and the public turned out in force. The city of Saint-Malo is buzzing with excitement, and Cap Fréhel, like the harbor itself, is teeming with people. The rest of the race will undoubtedly pique the public's curiosity, but what will cement this first edition in history is the finish between Mike Birch and Michel Malinovsky, with Birch winning by a mere 98 seconds after 23 days at sea and 3,500 nautical miles. Florence Arthaud, 21, who had given up everything a year earlier, finishes eleventh after 27 days at sea. She will be the first woman to finish and will be nicknamed "the little sweetheart of the Atlantic," a term she will detest. On a more tragic note, this edition will also see the disappearance at sea of Alain Colas, aboard his boat Manureva. Following a final call during which the navigator indicated he was caught in the center of a typhoon, neither the sailor nor the boat could be found after more than 250 hours of searching.

exergue.t: winning by a mere 98 seconds after 23 days at sea and 3,500 nautical miles

editions.resume: Large multihulls made their appearance, including Eugène Riguidel's William-Saurin (27 meters) and Marc Pajot's Elf Aquitaine. Three of them measured over 20 meters. Marc Pajot kept everyone in suspense: with a central beam cracked at the point of breaking, the sailor from La Baule led the race relentlessly and won by 10 hours over Bruno Peyron's Jaz. There were 19 retirements in this second edition, including Ian Johnston on his trimaran Rennie (capsize), Jean-Yves Terlain on Gauthier III (dismasting), Éric Tabarly on Paul Ricard, and Daniel Gillard on BAI Brittany Ferries.
editions.description: The 1978 edition made a lasting impression and generated considerable enthusiasm among sailors, who flocked to participate in the second edition in 1982. Fifty-two boats took the start, including a significant number of professional sailors, well-known to the public: Tabarly, Birch, Malinovsky, Peyron, Poupon, and others. The innovation lay in equipping all boats with Argos beacons, as well as the creation of a press center at the foot of the Montparnasse Tower, allowing for close monitoring of the competition. This edition was marked by particularly difficult conditions, forcing Éric Tabarly to abandon the race. Marc Pajot arrived victorious on the other side of the Atlantic, closely followed by Bruno Peyron, and finally Mike Birch. All three completed the podium in the multihull category. Notably, nine of the top ten boats in Guadeloupe were multihulls.

exergue.t: nine of the top ten boats in Guadeloupe were multihulls

editions.resume: Large multihulls dominated the 1986 edition: no fewer than 13 boats over 23 meters in Class 1. With a 48-hour lead over his direct competitors, Philippe Poupon on Fleury Michon VIII crossed the finish line. His foiling trimaran performed exceptionally well on the southern route and widened the gap with his pursuers. He dedicated his victory to the memory of his friend Loïc Caradec.
editions.description: Thirty-three boats are taking part in the 1986 edition. The best skippers are still present, even though the number of participants is down compared to 1982. The size of the boats, however, is ever more gigantic: 13 boats measure over 23 meters. Never before has the offshore race brought together such a fleet of giants. Among the entrants, the trend is decidedly towards catamarans with no fewer than 13 competing, compared to 9 trimarans, some of which are equipped with new appendages: foils. Depressions follow one another across the Atlantic and take a heavy toll on the Route du Rhum fleet. The weather conditions of the first few days severely test the competitors; retirements and damage follow one after another. Loïc Caradec, sailing aboard his imposing trimaran Royale II (22.60 meters), has gone silent. Florence Arthaud diverts to her position and discovers the overturned wreck with no signs of life. Loïc Caradec will never be found. This will be the second tragedy in the history of the Route du Rhum, eight years after the disappearance of Alain Colas. Despite this obvious upheaval, Philippe Poupon wins ahead of Bruno Peyron and Lionel Péan.

exergue.t: Never before has the offshore race brought together such a fleet of giants.

editions.resume: The 60-foot limit on boat size became the norm. Trimarans took hold. New, all-carbon boats appeared: weight reduction, stiffness, and strength seemed to be the winning combination. The major innovation of the 1990 edition was the arrival of GPS (Global Positioning System), which allowed each sailor to know their position in real time and import weather files. These files, after being combined with polar diagrams, speed, and heading, offered several possible routes to the sailors. Florence Arthaud on Pierre 1er had an incredible race. She won the Route du Rhum, alone against the ocean and a pack of pursuers. While Philippe Poupon finished second, third was a newcomer: Laurent Bourgnon.
editions.description: 1990 marked a year of change. Much had changed in the past four years, and the fleet was undergoing a transformation. Trimarans seemed to have definitively established themselves as the standard for solo racing, and the 60-foot limit was almost universally accepted. Backed into a corner, Bruno Peyron, Francis Joyon, and Hervé Laurent were refused entry to the Route du Rhum with their 65-foot boats. Joyon reduced the size of his hull by cutting off a section just days before the start, while Peyron and Laurent set off as "pirates," meaning without being included in the official rankings. Nevertheless, 31 competitors arrived in Saint-Malo, including new boats such as Pierre 1er (Florence Arthaud), Fujichrome (Mike Birch), RMO (Laurent Bourgnon), and Fleury Michon IX (Philippe Poupon). Laurent Bourgnon rounded the Cap Fréhel buoy in first place. The tone is set: they'll have to keep up with the pace set by these new Formula 1 boats of the seas. As is typical for November, storms batter the fleet, and damage begins to occur: Jean Maurel (Elf Aquitaine III) loses his mast, and Laurent Bourgnon's centerboard explodes, causing a leak. He says nothing, but pumps water… In Pointe-à-Pitre, Florence Arthaud, exhausted and having been without electronics and communication since the Azores, will enter Route du Rhum legend by becoming the first woman to win a solo offshore race.

exergue.t: the first woman to win a solo offshore race

editions.resume: Beyond the sailors' battle on the water, the advice of shore-based routers has taken on incredible importance, with, among others, Richard Silvani advising Laurent Bourgnon and Jean-Yves Bernot and Louis Bodin advising Paul Vatine. The new generation of 60-foot monohulls, with their ballast tanks, are showing incredible potential. While they can compete on equal terms with trimarans at certain points of sail, they have been able to cope with the elements more easily and can afford to carry more sail than before.
editions.description: Only 24 boats are taking part in this fifth edition, but in a major new development, there will be two races within the race: one for multihulls and one for monohulls. As fate would have it, there are the same number of entries in each category. And while many have images of Florence Arthaud etched in their minds, she won't be there to defend her title. Only her boat will be present, bought by billionaire Steve Fossett and renamed Lakota. But the battle across the fleet is no less spectacular. In the multihull class, Loïck Peron will be dismasted, and Paul Vatine will become the main rival of Laurent Bourgnon, who will win his first Route du Rhum. In the monohull class, Yves Parlier, Alain Gautier, and Halvard Mabire are the clear favorites. Mabire will lose his keel, capsize, and activate his distress beacon. He will be rescued after remaining in the icy water for more than ten hours. Yves Parlier and Alain Gautier will finish just behind the two leading trimarans, which will nonetheless remain a remarkable performance.

exergue.t: there will be two races within the race: one for multihulls and one for monohulls

editions.resume: Yves Parlier, seriously injured in a paragliding accident, entrusted his 60-foot Aquitaine Innovations to Thomas Coville. Coville won in the monohull class, navigated by Parlier himself. A great sailor was born! Ellen MacArthur also won in the monohull class aboard her Kingfisher. Despite repeated technical problems, the young Englishwoman challenged the 60-footers and captivated the public. Four sailors arrived neck and neck off the coast of Guadeloupe: Laurent Bourgnon, Alain Gautier, Marc Guillemot, and Franck Cammas. Who would win? The one who made the fewest mistakes, according to Alain Gautier. Laurent Bourgnon thus secured his second consecutive victory in the Route du Rhum.
editions.description: Nineteen multihulls versus eighteen monohulls: a fine lineup for the twentieth anniversary of the Route du Rhum. In six editions, this transatlantic race has become a major classic, a must for all professional sailors. Laurent Bourgnon is back to defend his title aboard an extremely reliable trimaran, with perfectly mastered mechanics, 24/7 French and American weather analysis via Richard Silvani and Bob Rice, and a fiercely competitive spirit. His main rival, who has his sights set on a first Route du Rhum victory, is none other than Loïck Peyron. The Atlantic becomes a veritable chessboard on which the greatest solo sailors are making their moves: Francis Joyon, Paul Vatine, Alain Gautier, Marc Guillemot, and Franck Cammas will keep everyone on the edge of their seats. Upon arriving in Guadeloupe, Laurent Bourgnon became the first sailor in the race's history to achieve a double victory, setting a new crossing time record of 12 days, 8 hours, and 41 minutes. Alain Gautier took second place, and Franck Cammas completed the podium, crossing the finish line just eight minutes ahead of Marc Guillemot. In the monohull category, Thomas Coville, called upon to replace Yves Parlier at the last minute following the latter's paragliding accident, triumphed over Jean-Luc Van Den Heede. Ellen MacArthur, then 22 years old, won the monohull race on her 50-foot boat, foreshadowing a brilliant career.

exergue.t: the first sailor in the race's history to achieve a double victory

editions.resume: The seventh edition was marked by a very deep depression that caused a devastating number of losses among the ORMA multihulls. Michel Desjoyeaux (Géant), Marc Guillemot (Biscuits La Trinitaine), and Lalou Roucayrol (Banque Populaire) were the only three to finish out of the 18 starters. Michel Etevenon, who had died a year earlier, was no longer with us. The new race organizing team decided to offer two staggered starts: one for the monohulls and one for the multihulls. Steve Ravussin, the Swiss skipper, the only sailor to emerge from the storm virtually unscathed, was sailing towards a victorious finish in Guadeloupe before being caught out by a squall. He capsized just 734 nautical miles (1,360 km) from Pointe-à-Pitre. This edition celebrates the victory of Ellen MacArthur in the IMOCA monohull and that of Michel Desjoyeaux in the ORMA trimaran, who, after three technical stops, took the lead in the rankings in a fierce battle with his pursuers.
editions.description: With 58 competitors at the start, 2002 was a record year. Not only in terms of participation, but also, unfortunately, in terms of retirements. While 28 boats finished the race, only 3 out of 18 reached the Caribbean in the ORMA class, the premier class of 60-foot multihulls. Franck Cammas was the first to fall victim to the depression that swept through the fleet at the start of the race, and only three of them made it across the Atlantic: Michel Desjoyeaux, the winner, followed by Marc Guillemot and Lalou Roucayrol (the only skipper to finish without stopping). Another historic first was the real-time arrival of two IMOCA monohulls ahead of the multihulls, including that of Ellen MacArthur and Mike Golding. This was a consequence of the staggered start of the monohulls, which had departed a day before the multihulls, and of capsizes and damage caused by the horrendous weather conditions encountered off La Coruña.

exergue.t: only 3 out of 18 reached the Caribbean in the ORMA class, the premier class of 60-foot multihulls

editions.resume: Seventy-four skippers lined up at the start, a record turnout for the race, including 25 Class40 entries, marking its debut in the competition. Sixty-two boats reached Guadeloupe, with 61 finishing, illustrating a resounding sporting success. 1.2 million visitors thronged the docks during the ten days preceding the start.
editions.description: This eighth edition of the famous solo transatlantic race will be remembered for Lionel Lemonchois' breathtaking sprint, winner of the premier 60-foot multihull category aboard Gitana 11. Sailing from Saint-Malo to Pointe-à-Pitre in 7 days, 17 hours, and 19 minutes, the Norman sailor shattered Laurent Bourgnon's previous record by more than four days, averaging a dizzying 19.11 knots solo! The other highlight of this edition was the epic duel between Roland Jourdain (Sill and Véolia) and Jean Le Cam (VM Matériaux) in the IMOCA class, resulting in a nail-biting finish. After 3,543 nautical miles, only 28 minutes separated them, allowing Jourdain to cement his place in Route du Rhum legend. Also, for the first time in the history of the Route du Rhum, 25 Class40s participated, bringing together professionals and amateurs. Phil Sharp will come in first in this category.

exergue.t: the Norman sailor shattered Laurent Bourgnon's previous record by more than four days

editions.resume: Nine Ultime trimarans, nine IMOCA trimarans, twelve Multi50 trimarans, eleven Route du Rhum trimarans, and forty-four Class40 trimarans—a total of 85 competitors—took part in a truly exceptional lineup. Two million viewers cheered on the sailors of the Route du Rhum. Franck Cammas joins the elite circle of winners of the queen of transatlantic races and celebrates, in his own unique way, the return of the giants of offshore racing.
editions.description: The 60-foot (18.28-meter) boat size limit imposed since 1990 has been abandoned, returning to the "no limit" concept that guided the race's creation in 1978. With 85 solo sailors at the starting line and nearly 2 million visitors, the 2010 Route du Rhum, from its departure from Saint-Malo, established itself as a record-breaking edition. Nine boats competed in the Ultim class, marking a highly anticipated return. There were also nine IMOCA boats, twelve Multi 50s, forty-four Class40s, and eleven Rhum class yachts. On the water, the spectacle lived up to expectations. Winner in Pointe-à-Pitre aboard his 31.50-meter trimaran, Franck Cammas, skipper of Groupama 3, entered the annals of sailing history, but fell short of the record time, completing the transatlantic crossing in 9 days, 3 hours, 14 minutes, and 47 seconds. Francis Joyon (Idec) and Thomas Coville (Sodebo) completed the podium. Two sailors particularly distinguished themselves by achieving a double victory: Roland Jourdain (Veolia Environnement), winner in the IMOCA class for the second consecutive year, and Lionel Lemonchois (Prince de Bretagne), who repeated his 2006 feat, this time winning on a 50-foot multihull. In Class40, Thomas Ruyant finished first in his category, while the Italian Andrea Mura won in the Rhum class.

exergue.t: the 2010 Route du Rhum, from its departure from Saint-Malo, established itself as a record-breaking edition

editions.resume: Eight Ultime trimarans, nine IMOCA trimarans, eleven Multi50 trimarans, twenty Route du Rhum trimarans, and forty-three Class40 trimarans—a total of 91 competitors—took part in a top-notch lineup. Yann Guichard embarked on the transatlantic race aboard Spindrift 2, his 40-meter-long and 23-meter-wide trimaran with 800 square meters of sail area. He arrived just a few hours after the winner. François Gabart shattered the monohull record, completing the race in 12 days and 4 hours, leading from start to finish. 1.35 million visitors flocked to the race villages.
editions.description: For its tenth edition in 2014, the Route du Rhum - Destination Guadeloupe continued to break records. Firstly, on the sporting front, with 91 sailboats gathered on the same starting line off Saint-Malo on November 2nd at 2:00 PM, and upon arrival in Guadeloupe, a magnificent winner, Loïck Peyron, who set a new record time, completing the 3,542 nautical mile course in 7 days, 15 hours, 8 minutes, and 32 seconds. Secondly, on the media front, with unprecedented coverage including over 67 hours of television broadcasts, over 44 hours of radio reports, more than 5,500 press articles, over 900 accredited journalists, and over 12,000 online articles. Finally, between the start of the corsair city and the Place de la Victoire in Pointe-à-Pitre, more than 2,200,000 people came to stroll through the start and finish villages and taste the magic of Rum!

exergue.t: the Route du Rhum - Destination Guadeloupe continued to break records.

editions.titre: A spectacular finish: Gabart vs Joyon!
editions.resume: An anniversary year that broke all participation records since the race's inception: 123 sailors were registered. Naval architects Marc Van Pethegem and Vincent Lauriot-Prévost (VPLP) secured their eighth consecutive victory with their multihull designs. Following Florence Arthaud's triumph in 1990, they have continuously designed the boats for every winner of the Route du Rhum - Destination Guadeloupe. And for the third time in a row, the maxi trimaran skippered by Franck Cammas in 2010, Loïck Peyron in 2014, and Francis Joyon in 2018, emerged victorious!
editions.description: A 40th anniversary celebration, a huge crowd in Saint-Malo. A spectacular start between Pointe du Grouin and Cap Fréhel. Exceptional enthusiasm from internet users and social media. A thrilling finale among the Ultims and an incredible turnaround in the IMOCA monohulls. Crossing records shattered in four out of six categories, a new ranking with the Rhum Mono, a strong international presence, and a legendary 3,542-mile course… A record number of participants with 123 boats and increased attendance compared to 2014: 1.35 million people! Twelve days of festivities culminated in the iconic passage through the locks, reaching a stretch of water swept by a pleasant 15-knot southeasterly breeze on Sunday, November 4, 2018, at 2:00 PM – ideal conditions for setting off towards Guadeloupe. The eleventh edition of the Route du Rhum - Destination Guadeloupe will be remembered for years to come. The arrival of the Ultims was thrilling, with the duel between Francis Joyon and François Gabart ultimately seeing Joyon prevail by a few hundred meters, with a time difference of 428 seconds. Alex Thomson, in the IMOCA class, who had been leading the fleet, fell asleep just meters from the tip of Guadeloupe and, exhausted, ran aground on the rocks 60 miles from the finish. He crossed the finish line first, but was forced to pull himself out using his engine, resulting in a 24-hour penalty. The victory ultimately went to Paul Meilhat, ahead of Yann Éliès and Alex Thomson.

exergue.t: A thrilling finale among the Ultims and an incredible turnaround in the IMOCA monohulls.

editions.description: The 12th edition of the Route du Rhum - Destination Guadeloupe promised to be sensational. It was even more so. And with good reason: with 138 competitors at the starting line – the largest and most impressive fleet ever assembled for an ocean race – one of the most glorious chapters in the history of the most legendary of solo transatlantic races has undoubtedly just been written. "This 2022 edition was shaping up to be one for the record books, and it lived up to all expectations. The naval battle was on full display, at every level. The race lived up to its reputation, with tough and challenging conditions that opened up the competition to the highest level," stated Joseph Bizard, Managing Director of OC Sport Pen Duick, who was delighted with the spectacle on the water and also with the vitality of the different classes and categories of boats, which confirms the unique character of the Route du Rhum – Destination Guadeloupe. An exceptional event. The race is a major event in offshore racing, and this 12th edition distinguished itself even more than previous ones in every aspect. In the opinion of everyone—sailors, owners, partners, and the public—it was special and, in a way, marked a kind of shift, like a ratchet effect, becoming a race of excellence across all classes and categories. "Crossing the North Atlantic in November is certainly no small feat (as a reminder: of the 138 solo sailors who started, 103 managed to reach Pointe-à-Pitre). It is a difficult challenge that justifies the exceptional nature of the race and makes it so exciting," added the Managing Director of OC Sport Pen Duick. Indeed, the magic worked in a big way. A source of satisfaction for the organizers, whose aim was to make the event a time for bringing together sailors and the general public. An event to bring people together. In Saint-Malo, the 70,000 m² village was designed to showcase the entire fleet. Significant work was also done on ergonomics to ensure easy and comfortable access. This allowed for a huge number of visitors and provided exciting entertainment, such as parades and lock passages. At the same time, integrating sustainable development principles into the event gave even more meaning to the various initiatives undertaken and fully served as a platform for impact and a sounding board to inform, raise awareness, and promote major environmental issues related to the ocean. "The foundations we have laid open up great possibilities for building future editions." A successful "opera." Although it is still a little too early to draw any definitive quantitative conclusions, an initial trend is emerging, and, good news, it confirms the appeal of offshore racing itself. "It's a discipline that appeals to, captivates, and inspires passion." We were able to witness its remarkable power of attraction through the various channels we had set up to follow the race. This 12th edition of the Route du Rhum - Destination Guadeloupe was, without a doubt, a grand celebration of the sea and boats,” affirmed the representative of OC Sport Pen Duick. Indeed, this 2022 edition lived up to the initial promise made by Michel Etevenon who, it should be remembered, stated that his “intention was not to organize a race but to stage an opera.”

exergue.t: his “intention was not to organize a race but to stage an opera.”

intertitres: An event to bring people together.
